ing: peeled, cut into chunks, woody core removed
st: Peel the yam, cassava and plantains and cut them into even chunks. Cut out the tough fibrous core of the cassava.
Put everything in a large pot, cover with water and add [[0.5 tsp]] salt.
Bring to a boil, then simmer until all the pieces are very soft when pierced with a fork.
Meanwhile, stir [[3 tbsp]] peanut butter with [[1.5 cup]] hot water in a small pan, add the chopped chili and [[0.5 tsp]] salt, and simmer gently.
Drain the cooked roots, keeping a little cooking water. Mash them in a sturdy bowl with a potato masher, or pound with a wooden pestle in a mortar.
Work the mash hard, adding a splash of the cooking water if needed, until it becomes a smooth, stretchy dough with no lumps.
With wet hands, shape the dough into four smooth balls.
Serve each ball with warm peanut chili dip, or with any soup or stew.
Whisk the cornmeal, cassava flour and [[1 cup]] cold water in a bowl into a smooth paste. (Traditionally the corn is fermented for a day or two; this is a quick version.)
Bring [[2 cups]] water and [[0.5 tsp]] salt to a boil in a heavy pot.
Pour in the paste, stirring constantly, and cook over medium heat until very thick.
Turn the heat to low and keep stirring hard with a wooden spoon, pressing out lumps, until the dough pulls away from the pot.
Wet a bowl, scoop in the dough and turn it out as one smooth ball. Keep warm.
For the sauce, heat the oil in a pan and cook the onion and chili for 4 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, okra, [[1 cup]] water and [[0.5 tsp]] salt. Simmer until the okra is tender and the sauce is thick.
Serve the dough in slices or balls with the sauce spooned over.
Put the beef in a pot with [[2 cups]] water, half the onion and [[0.5 tsp]] salt. Simmer until the beef is tender.
Heat the palm oil in a large pan over medium heat.
Cook the remaining onion and the chili for 4 minutes until soft.
Add the tomatoes and cook until they break down into a thick sauce.
Add the beef with its broth and simmer for 5 minutes.
Stir in the spinach in batches until wilted, then add the fish and [[0.5 tsp]] salt.
Simmer gently, uncovered, until the spinach is soft and the fish is cooked through.
Taste, adjust salt, and serve with rice, fufu or akoumé.
If using fresh jute leaves, strip them from the stems and wash well. Chop finely. Thaw frozen leaves first.
Bring [[1.5 cups]] water to a boil in a pot, add the leaves and the baking soda if using.
Simmer until the leaves are tender and the broth turns slippery and thick.
In a pan, heat the palm oil and cook the onion and chili until soft.
Add the tomatoes and cook until they form a thick paste.
Stir the tomato mixture and the fish into the leaves.
Season with [[0.75 tsp]] salt and simmer on low, stirring now and then.
Serve hot with fufu, akoumé or rice.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat and cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the ginger and chili and stir for 1 minute.
Add the chicken, tomatoes, [[4 cups]] water and the salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer, covered.
Put the peanut butter in a bowl and whisk in a ladle of hot broth until smooth.
Stir the peanut mixture into the pot and simmer, uncovered, on low heat.
Stir often so the soup does not stick, and skim off any oil that rises.
Check that the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C) and is falling off the bone. Taste and adjust salt.
Serve hot with rice or fufu.
Blend the chilies, ginger, onion, garlic, [[2 tbsp]] oil and salt into a coarse paste.
Cut deep slashes in the chicken so the marinade can soak in.
Rub the paste all over the chicken, working it into the slashes.
Cover and marinate in the fridge.
Heat a grill or the oven to 400°F (200°C). Brush the chicken with [[1 tbsp]] oil.
Cook, turning sometimes, until the skin is browned and charred in spots.
Check that the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C) and the juices run clear.
Rest for 5 minutes and serve with fried yam, plantain or fresh onion and tomato.
Whisk the rice flour, cornmeal, yeast, sugar and salt in a large bowl.
Slowly stir in [[2.5 cups]] warm water to make a thick, smooth batter like pancake batter.
Cover and let it rest in a warm place until puffy and bubbly.
Lightly grease small ramekins or a muffin tin with the oil.
Set a rack or steamer basket in a big pot with about [[1 inch]] water and bring to a boil.
Stir the batter once and fill the molds about three-quarters full.
Steam covered over medium heat until a toothpick comes out clean. Do not lift the lid often.
Cool for 5 minutes, then unmold. Serve warm with fish stew, pepper sauce or fried fish.
Mix the cornmeal, [[1 cup]] water and the salt into a dough, cover, and let it sour in a warm spot for a day if you like a tangy taste. Skip the souring for a quick version.
Soak the husks in hot water until soft, then pat dry.
Cook the dough in a pot with [[1.5 cups]] water, stirring hard, until thick and smooth.
Cool a few minutes. With wet hands, shape handfuls into oval dumplings.
Wrap each dumpling in two husks and tie with a strip of husk.
Steam the packets in a covered pot over simmering water.
Meanwhile, heat the oil, cook the onion and chili for 4 minutes, then add tomatoes and fish and cook for 10 minutes.
Unwrap the dumplings and serve with the fish sauce.
Stir the cornmeal with [[1 cup]] cold water until smooth. For the traditional tang, cover and leave in a warm spot to ferment for a day.
Bring [[2 cups]] water and the salt to a boil in a saucepan.
Whisk in the cornmeal mixture and keep whisking so no lumps form.
Lower the heat and cook, stirring often, until the pudding is thick and glossy.
Stir in half of the sugar and let the pudding cool completely.
Thin with a splash of water if it is too stiff; it should be spoonable.
Serve in bowls topped with cold milk, remaining sugar and ice.

ing: divided: 3 cups for frying, 1 tbsp for the sauce
st: Peel the yam and cut it into thick sticks. Rinse and drain well.
Boil the yam in salted water with [[1 tsp]] salt for 5 minutes, then drain and pat dry. This keeps the inside soft.
For the pepper sauce, heat [[1 tbsp]] oil and cook half the onion and the chilies for 3 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and [[0.5 tsp]] salt and cook until thick and saucy. Keep warm.
Heat [[3 cups]] oil in a deep pot to 350°F (175°C).
Fry the yam in batches until golden and crisp outside.
Drain on paper towels and sprinkle with a little salt.
Serve hot with the pepper sauce and the remaining raw onion.
